# 研究任务：表格模型上 SHAP 特征归因的重复运行可靠性

## 问题与动机

SHAP 被广泛用于为高风险场景（信贷、医疗等）中的模型决策提供理由。在实际部署中，
SHAP 通常依赖随机近似算法估计，并受计算预算限制，因此同一个训练好的模型、同一个
输入实例，多次运行解释器可能得到不同的归因向量。

实践中常见的做法是对一个实例只运行一次解释器，并把所得特征归因作为该预测的依据。
这种做法在什么条件下足够可靠、在什么条件下不够可靠，目前缺少系统的实证证据。
我们希望你研究这一问题，并保留部署中真实的计算预算这一约束。

请自行确定并论证具体的研究问题与方法。研究需要回答：对一个训练好的表格模型，
单次运行所得的 SHAP 特征归因在多大程度上可以被当作该预测的可靠依据；这一判断需要依据
哪些度量和比较标准；结论在哪些条件下成立、在哪些条件下不成立。

## 期望

- 设计可复现的实验方法，在多个公开表格数据集和多种模型上系统验证，

- 明确你的实验设置（数据、模型、计算预算）和统计处理方式，并说明选择理由。

# Brief — the idea

## Question
When a trained tabular model's prediction is "justified" by one run of a randomised SHAP estimator under a deployment-sized budget, **for which instances, models, datasets and budgets is that one run a reliable basis for the conclusions a reader draws from it** (which features are top, in what order, with which sign) — and can the user *know* this from the single run alone?

The study does not ask "is SHAP noisy?" (it is, at low budget). It asks where the noise changes a **decision-relevant conclusion**, against what yardstick, and whether the single run can certify itself.

## What prior work leaves open
- Estimator papers (Kernel SHAP, unbiased Kernel SHAP + variance estimates, permutation / antithetic sampling, Leverage SHAP, regression-adjusted MC, SHAP-IQ) report error to the exact Shapley value, mostly in L2 / MSE, on average over instances, at *chosen* budgets. They do not ask whether top-k / ranking / sign conclusions of one run survive, instance by instance, at *deployment default* budgets.
- Disagreement / robustness / LIME-stability work (Krishna et al., Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola, Visani et al.) compares *methods* or perturbed inputs; the repeat-run variability of one fixed explainer on one fixed model+instance is not separated from method choice, background choice, or model retraining.
- Background-size stability (Yuan et al.) is for deep models only and does not separate sampling noise from the change of the value function.
- Rashomon / predictive-multiplicity work gives a natural yardstick (variability from equally accurate retrained models) but has not been used to *calibrate* explainer noise.

## Contribution (what the paper claims to add)
1. **A protocol with an exact reference.** For each model/instance the Shapley value of the *same* value function (same background) is computed exactly (enumeration for d ≤ ~16–20; closed form for linear; exact interventional TreeSHAP for trees). Explainer randomness is therefore separated from the definition of the attribution (background, true-to-model vs true-to-data), and error is measured to ground truth, not only run-to-run.
2. **Decision-relevant reliability metrics and yardsticks.** Top-1 identity, top-k set agreement (Jaccard; Nogueira stability across runs), rank agreement (RBO, Kendall), sign-flip rate of top features, relative L2 — each judged against three noise floors: (a) explainer-run noise vs (b) background-resampling noise vs (c) retrain-seed (Rashomon-style) noise of the model. "Reliable" is defined as: with probability ≥ 1−δ over explainer randomness, the top-k conclusion equals the exact one (thresholds stated up front, with sensitivity analysis).
3. **A map of conditions.** Reliability as a function of budget (coalition samples × background rows, measured in model evaluations), estimator (Kernel SHAP default, paired / unbiased variants, permutation sampling, Leverage SHAP), model family (logistic regression, random forest, gradient-boosted trees, MLP), dimension (d = 8 … 279), and an instance-level covariate — the **attribution margin** (gap between adjacent ranked |φ|, relative to noise) — which we hypothesise is the main driver. Includes the regime that is trivial (budget ≥ 2^d ⇒ exact, e.g. ACS-Income d=10 at default shap budget) so that "reliable" findings are not artefacts of low d.
4. **A deployable single-run check.** Test whether within-run quantities (Kernel SHAP's bootstrap / paired-sample variance estimate, with the margin) predict the repeated-run top-k instability and the exact error, i.e. whether one run can flag itself, and derive a minimum-budget rule validated on held-out datasets. If it cannot, that negative result is reported.

# How the study relates to prior work

**Shapley attribution and its estimators.** SHAP (Lundberg & Lee 2017) casts feature attribution as Shapley values of a
value function defined by removing features; the value function can be marginal or conditional
(Chen et al. 2020; Sundararajan & Najmi 2020; Kumar et al. 2020; Covert et al. 2020 unify removal-based explanations).
Model-agnostic estimation is randomised: Kernel SHAP and its unbiased variant with variance/convergence estimates
(Covert & Lee 2021), permutation / antithetic sampling (Mitchell et al. 2022), Leverage SHAP with guarantees
(Musco & Witter 2025), regression-adjusted MC (Witter et al. 2025), SHAP-IQ (Fumagalli et al. 2023); an overview in Chen et al. 2023.
Trees admit deterministic TreeSHAP (Lundberg et al. 2020). These works measure error to the exact Shapley value
(typically L2, averaged over instances, at chosen budgets). **Gap:** whether one run at a deployment budget supports the
decision-relevant conclusions drawn from it, instance by instance, is not studied; nor whether the run can detect its own failure.

**Explanation disagreement and robustness.** Krishna et al. 2022 and Neely et al. 2021 study disagreement *between* methods;
Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola 2018 and Ghorbani et al. 2019 study sensitivity to input perturbation; Visani et al. 2022 study LIME stability
under resampling; Yuan et al. 2022 study background size for deep models. **Difference:** we fix model, value function and instance
and isolate the explainer's own randomness against an exact reference, and compare it to background and retraining noise.

**Multiplicity yardsticks.** Marx et al. 2020 (predictive multiplicity), Fisher et al. 2019 and Dong & Rudin 2020 (model class reliance), Rashomon importance
distribution (Rashomon-set literature) give the variability between equally accurate models; we use it as a noise floor for
explainer noise, not as the target.

**Metrics.** Stability of selected sets (Nogueira et al. 2018) and indefinite-ranking similarity (RBO; Webber et al. 2010) for top-k conclusions.

**Data and models.** Ding et al. 2021 (folktables/ACS), German Credit (UCI), Gorishniy et al. 2021 for tabular deep models.

*Must cite / compare:* all above. *Not to cite as found by this role:* any item not in `*.bib`; Dong & Rudin 2020 is a pointer
(Nature MI, doi 10.1038/s42256-020-00264-0 found in search) and still needs its bib entry; fetch before use.

mkdir -p reviews && cat > reviews/idea-review-1.md <<'EOF'
# Review 1 of the idea (Brief @ wiki rev of 2026-11-25 16:53, positioning @ bfb73c8)

Reviewed against `Research objective` (idea-review-repo#1). The plan of the study (`Outline`) is not written yet, so this
review covers the idea; the plan is reviewed when the outline exists.

## What is strong (keep)
- The question is the right one: it moves from "SHAP is noisy" to "where does noise change a conclusion a reader draws, and can the run know it". This answers the objective's three asks (how reliable, by what measure/yardstick, under which conditions).
- Exact reference for the *same* value function separates explainer randomness from definition of the attribution. This is the main source of rigor and the thing prior estimator papers do not do at top-k level.
- Three noise floors, falsifiable H1-H4 with "any of reliable / conditional / unreliable is acceptable", the trivial-regime control (ACS-Income d=10 ⇒ exact at default budget), and bootstrap over instances are all good.

## Weaknesses, in order of how much they threaten the paper

### 1. The compute plan does not fit the 24 CPU-hour envelope (planning estimate, measured throughput only for the unit cost)
I timed the unit cost in this sandbox: 200k model evaluations of a 100-tree random forest (20 features, 1 core) take 1.4 s; an MLP 0.6 s.
One Kernel SHAP run at shap's default (2d+2048 ≈ 2088 coalitions × 100 background rows) is ≈ 2·10^5 evaluations ≈ 1.4 s for RF.
Brief grid: 150 instances × R=30 repeats × ~5 budgets × ~5 estimators = ~110k runs per (dataset, model) ⇒ ~45-60 CPU-h for *one* RF on *one* dataset at the default-order budget (the grid goes above default). With 4 models × 5 datasets the grid is >20× the envelope. The brief says "total fits" without a calculation.
**Make stronger, not narrower:** write a cost table (evaluations per run × runs) before committing; make the core grid small and complete (e.g. 2-3 main datasets × 3-4 models × 4 budgets × Kernel SHAP default + one paired/permutation variant, R and instances sized by the CI width needed), and declare estimators 4-5 (Leverage, regression-adjusted MC, SHAP-IQ) and Arrhythmia as a labelled secondary slice on a few instances. Cheap tricks that keep rigor: evaluate all budgets from nested samples of one stream; reuse the model-evaluation cache across repeats when coalitions repeat; run the exact reference once per instance; sub-sample background to the *definition* budget (e.g. 50-100 rows) and hold it fixed.

### 2. Exact reference is not feasible as written for several cells
- Enumeration over 2^d coalitions × B background rows: d=20 ⇒ 10^6 × 100 = 10^8 evaluations per instance (≈ 10 min for RF/MLP, ×150 instances, ×models) — not "enumeration for d ≤ ~16-20". Realistically exact-by-enumeration for black-box models is d ≤ ~14-16 (ACS Employment d=16 borderline). German Credit d=20 and ACS Public Coverage d=19 are exact only for linear (closed form) and trees (interventional TreeSHAP). For MLP at d≥17 the reference is a very-high-budget run, which is *not* exact and must be treated as the Arrhythmia case is (flagged, with its own error bar, and its self-noise subtracted/bounded). Say which cells have which kind of reference.
- Feature unit: German Credit's "d=20" is raw attributes; one-hot encoding gives ~48 columns and a different game. Fix the unit (grouped categorical = one player, which is also what a loan officer reads) and say so; same for ACS categoricals.
- Output space: TreeSHAP for GBMs explains the raw log-odds; Kernel SHAP on `predict_proba` explains probability. Rankings and signs can differ between them. Choose one output space per model family and use it for both exact and estimated values (log-odds for all models if possible), or the "error to exact" mixes value-function mismatch with noise — exactly the confound the paper claims to remove.

shown.message:
I reviewed the idea and sent the review to `idea-repo` as issue #3. I haven't reviewed the plan yet, because story-repo hasn't written the Outline. I'll review the plan when it appears.

The question is well chosen and the idea is worth building on. Its exact reference for the same value function is the strongest part. As written, it is over-scoped for the compute and has definition gaps a reviewer could use to dispute the main claim.

- **Compute:** I timed 200k model evaluations of a 100-tree random forest at 1.4 s on one core. The planned grid then costs roughly 45–60 CPU-hours for one random forest on one dataset. The brief claims the whole study fits in about 24 CPU-hours, which looks more than 20 times too small. The review asks for a cost table and a smaller complete core grid. That is a planning estimate from this timing, not a measurement of the full grid.
- **Exact reference:** Enumerating all feature subsets is not feasible for d=19–20 black-box models. German Credit's "d=20" also depends on how categorical features are grouped. TreeSHAP explains log-odds while Kernel SHAP on probabilities explains a different quantity, so mixing them confounds noise with definition.
- **"Reliable":** Near-ties make the exact top-k itself unstable, so the metric needs a tolerance-aware variant. With 30 repeats, per-instance 95% certification is impossible. The review also asks to separate single-run correctness from run-to-run agreement.
- **Retrain yardstick:** Its definition decides whether H3 comes out true or false, and the three noise floors must use the same metric to be comparable.
- **Single-run certificate:** The margin it uses must be one computed from the run itself, not the exact one. The brief also lacks the obvious competitor, which is running twice and comparing at equal total budget.
- **Statistics:** The unit of generalisation is the dataset, and only two to five datasets are planned.
- **Positioning:** Kolpaczki et al.'s "Shapley Bandits" for top-k identification is missing from the related work. I read only its title and abstract.

My commitment is recorded as `idea-review-repo`#2. The full review text is in `reviews/idea-review-1.md` in my repo, pushed as commit `4ecde59`.
